newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Strong Irish credit raises rate rise risk - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Strong Irish credit raises rate rise risk - analysts.

text.p: Strong lending growth in November has added to the risk of an Irish interest rate rise although most analysts say the central bank is likely to monitor the performance of the Irish pound and Irish inflation for a little longer before making any move to dampen credit growth.
Figures released on Thursday showed that the adjusted annual rate of growth in private sector credit rose to 16.4 percent in November from a revised 14.4 percent in October.
The November growth rate was well above broker forecasts which ranged from 14.0 to 14.5 percent.
"It's a bit of a shocker. It's certainly a good deal stronger than generally expected," Dermot O'Brien, economist at NCB Stockbrokers told Reuters.

Analysts noted there were a number of specific factors contributing to the sharp increase including a rise in lending to the Agricultural Intervention Agency and borrowing to fund tax payments which fuelled non-mortgage Irish pound credit in particular.
"Even stripping that out it doesn't explain the whole thing. You can't write it off and on that basis it will certainly create a bit of nervousness in the money market," O'Brien said.
Dealers noted that interbank rates from three months out had tightened by about a sixteenth following release of the data.
But economists said the central bank was unlikely to make any immediate move to raise interest rates.

"At the very least, I would imagine they would want to look into it a bit more to see if they can explain it and if there are other once-off or specific factors behind it. Or even just wait awhile and see if this is indeed a new trend or one-month volatility," NCB's O'Brien said.
Riada economist Padhraic Garvey said the November lending figures had increased the risk of a rate rise but the performance of the Irish pound was likely to be the crucial factor in this decision.
He noted that the economy was continuing to grow strongly, that a recent Irish wage accord allowed for pay increases and fiscal policy is set to be expansionary.

"The only factor holding inflation down is the strong currency. If there was any indication that the currency was to fall or was falling it would bring the bank closer to the interest rate hike trigger," he said.

Alan McQuaid, economist at Bloxham Stockbrokers, noted that the central bank must implement the interest and exchange rate policies that will enable Ireland to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"Given the continued strong growth in both house prices and credit demand, we believe that Irish retail interest rates will be increased by 25 basis points before the end of the first quarter," he said.
"Further monetary tightening, albeit fairly small, cannot be ruled out later in the year if inflation shows signs of getting out of hand."
